explanation: Fires on the verb or subject word in phrases describing that something is wrong, abnormal or happening unexpectedly, especially just before 'wrong'/'on'/'happening' (e.g. 'what am I [doing] wrong', 'something [went] wrong', 'what is [going] on', 'Is there [something] fishy'). Weak, scattered activations on biomedical words about abnormality or malfunction.

Fires on word-internal subword fragments in the middle of long technical or scientific words, mostly chemical, biomedical and botanical (e.g. 'beta[-c]ryptoxanthin', 'doc[os]ahexaenoic', '[poly]unsaturated', 'Fol[lic]ular'), and also on Russian 'what is my mistake / what could be the problem' phrases and 'something [feels] off'. These are separate jobs.

Fires on function words or verbs right after a reasoning or necessity frame that leads into a consequence or requirement ('Hence any drug [that]', 'I would have to [choose]', 'it is important to [understand]', 'therefore, students need to be [able]', 'it is assumed [that]'). The token itself matters less than the preceding 'thus/therefore/need to/have to' context. Activation is diffuse.

Fires on words and subwords expressing mutual, substitute or opposing relations ('substitute', 'each [other]', 'into [another]', 'opposite', 'complement', 'interactive', 'potentiate') and on chemistry/biomedical word fragments such as 'hydro[ly]sis', 'sup[ram]olecular', 'est[er]'. The two clusters do not clearly share a meaning.

Strongest on digits in the middle of long numbers in arithmetic or math problem text (e.g. 'prime factors of 2688592. 2, 16[8]037'). Below about 40% it fires weakly on varied tokens in code, prose and other languages with no clear pattern.

Fires on tokens in programming and technical Q&A contexts. It is strongest on the Go 'package' keyword after license or build-tag headers, and moderate on 'as' in Python 'with open(...) as', and on technical nouns in coding questions ('public [key]', '[decoder]', 'comments'). It also fires on a few unrelated tokens such as ANOVA fragments and Japanese text.

Fires on function words such as prepositions, articles and pronouns that come after comparison or relation frames ('as natural as [seeing]', 'like [never] before', 'much [like]', 'threats [to]', 'partnering [with]', 'in sync [with]'), plus some song titles and code tokens. The common thread is weak, so new snippets are hard to predict.

Fires on modifiers or nouns that name a physiological or technical quantity or magnitude in biomedical and engineering text, especially 'high' before a rate or volume ('high [tidal] volumes', '[high] morbidity', '[high] density', 'lethal dose', 'increase [the] risk', 'reduces the [data] size'). Strongest in medical-scientific abstracts.

A mixture: 'the [following] disclaimer' in BSD license headers, C/R code tokens ('#define [printf]', '[filter](', '[super]'), the ends of sentences, name subwords, and short text in other languages. No single shared feature.

Fires on the token that ends a module, class or name identifier: Elixir 'defmodule X [do]', 'Data[Frame]', 'pd', TV call signs in datelines ('([WXYZ])'), CJK characters for surnames, and subword pieces of foreign proper names ('Ir[ig]oyen', 'G[iov]anni'). The common theme is weak: name or identifier completion.

Fires on tokens inside or right after proper names (subword pieces of people's surnames such as 'Shard[ha]', 'Dumerv[il]', 'Dillash[aw]', and place or organization names) and on boilerplate tokens in code and license headers ('Oracle and[/or]', '$QT_BEGIN_LICENSE:LGPL3[$]', '#define fi first[newline]'). Diffuse otherwise.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word that has been split into several tokens, especially word-initial fragments like 'en'/'is'/'e'/'Ste'/'F' that begin rare chemical, medical or proper-name words ('is[opro]terenol', '[en]graft', '[en]ucleated', '[en]emas', 'Herr [Ste]ibel', 'St[.F]rancis'). The context of a rare multi-token word matters more than the fragment itself.

Fires on plural or mass nouns that name the components or contents of something, often after a container or quantity frame ('columns', 'data [fields]', 'contains [enzymes]', '50% [sugar]', '51 [people]', 'Tumor [cells]', 'in [pixels]'), in both code and prose. Moderately diffuse.

Fires on the numerator or exponent token inside LaTeX fractions and superscripts, especially the exponent in '\frac{...^[2]}{...}' and the start of a numerator after '\frac{'. Weak firing on digits of years after 'Copyright (c)' and on section numbers in '{#Sec1}'.
